compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In a fictional review of a new customer support system, either person can ask practical questions, suggest an unusual test or follow a written checklist. Those actions may reflect what the review requires.

The shared E describes a preference for directing attention and energy outward. It does not establish how quickly either person starts or how much they speak.

The shared P describes a preference for keeping outward options open to new information. Either person can follow a required process and explore an alternative within the permitted scope.

Keep the information and decision questions separate. What did someone notice in the evidence? Which considerations mattered when they chose a response? Both people can find patterns, verify details, use consistent criteria and consider the people affected.

One common mismatch has to be taken apart here: do not assign rule questions to T and interface questions to F. In this fictional review, both people have the same requirements, support-call records and decision rights. One reading looks for combinations where rules could conflict. Another checks where a support agent actually paused and what the screen showed. These illustrate S/N. Both readers can then evaluate each change against consistent criteria and its effects on agents and customers.

An anticipated conflict may warrant a test. A recorded pause may warrant checking what caused it. Both forms of evidence have limits. Either person can raise either concern.

Boundary of use: what follows is an invented test-team collaboration and an evening with friends, covering only how people talk and sort information. Decide who runs or reviews a check based on knowledge of the workflow and authority to act. Either person can explore a scenario, check a record or assess how the change would affect users.

In this fictional review, both people assess the same order lookup, address change, refund and handover requirements. Either can propose a case based on possible interactions between rules and can also verify what happens in a representative customer conversation.

A set of unusual cases can leave routine work unchecked. A set of routine cases can miss an interaction between rules. Compare what each case covers and which questions remain open.

Match each fictional case to the requirement or risk it addresses, and record whether it has been run and what was observed. A case count alone does not show coverage.

Record which issue concerns the interaction between rules and which concerns the workflow. Then agree what evidence the team needs to decide. The two questions can apply to the same change.

Each person can apply shared criteria and consider the people affected. Whether an objection concerns a rule or a screen does not distinguish Thinking from Feeling.

### ENTP and ESFP: the third round of a new board game, two readings of one rule

In this fictional board game, six players find two plausible readings of a rule. Anyone can check the wording or see how a reading plays out in the same board position.

Both carry a cost: whoever digs into the text spends ten minutes while the table starts scrolling phones; whoever plays first finds halfway through that the two sides have been scoring under different rules.

Comparing interpretations and observing what happens are ways of gathering information. Asking whether a reading is consistent and whether it works for the players are ways of weighing a choice. Either person can ask all four questions.

The check: the moment a dispute starts, agree which reading this round scores by, have both sides replay the same position once and see where the gap lands, then look up the original rule or ask the designer afterwards. That at least keeps the round going and leaves a record that can be checked, rather than resting on who concedes first.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
Taking full of ideas and fond of arguing as a marker of one type is the most common mismatch in this pair. Someone who invents three ways round a problem in a minute is often first thinking how to get this call finished, and that reaction turns up on both sides.

Liking to talk is no better as a dividing line. E says only that attention turns outward more often, not that anyone talks a lot, and there are quiet people in both types. If a comparison is wanted, look at what the talking is usually about: how else the rule could work, or what actually happened on that last order — and even that is only a tendency, not a test.

Whether a reviewer departs from a script depends on the task and the agreed test plan. Either can document a hypothesis and record what was actually observed.
